own_scenes.desc: Sylvia Robinson, la «madre del hip hop», venía del R&B: Little Sylvia, el dúo Mickey & Sylvia («Love Is Strange», 1956), la producción del «It’s Gonna Work Out Fine» de Ike & Tina, el sello All Platinum con su marido Joe (con supuestos lazos mafiosos) y su propio éxito «Pillow Talk» (1973). Arruinada, vio a Lovebug Starski en Harlem World en 1979 y quiso grabar aquello; con Morris Levy fundaron Sugar Hill. Su hijo la llevó a una pizzería de Nueva Jersey donde Big Bank Hank, mánager de los Cold Crush, hizo una audición en su coche junto a Master Gee y Wonder Mike: la Sugarhill Gang. Sobre una recreación de «Good Times» de Chic grabaron quince minutos de rimas que una radio de St. Louis, WESL, se atrevió a poner: «Rapper’s Delight» inundó el mundo en otoño de 1979, dejó en anécdota el «King Tim III» de Fatback y demostró que el hip hop era negocio. En el Bronx sonaba a imitación higienizada: Hank rapeaba las rimas de Grandmaster Caz («I’m the C-A-S-AN, the O-V-A»), un estribillo de Hollywood y una frase de Rahiem; «hizo retroceder el hip hop cinco años» (Charlie Chase). Para Kool Moe Dee, sin Sugar Hill quizá no habría industria. La casa no pagaba bien a sus artistas, y su banda (Skip Alexander, Doug Wimbish, Duke Bootee) tocaba los temas. En Harlem, Bobby Robinson y su sello Enjoy ficharon a Flash, los Funky 4 + 1 y los Treacherous Three.

refs.q: I’m like, What in the world is this?
refs.para: Jim Gates, my program director and general manager, walks into the control room and he’s carrying this album. He handed it to me, I put it on the turntable, and I dropped the needle on it, and all of a sudden it’s like, “I said a hip-hop, the hippie the hippie.” I’m like, What in the world is this?
refs.chapter: Cap. 3: What in the World Is This?

refs.q: And unlike punk rock—the revolution that failed—rap was going to be the revolution that succeeded.
refs.para: Bill Adler (journalist, Def Jam publicist): With rock [and] R&B running out of gas, and the pop music universe segregated by race, it was a perfect moment for this new rap music to emerge. And unlike punk rock—the revolution that failed—rap was going to be the revolution that succeeded.
refs.chapter: Cap. 3: What in the World Is This?

refs.q: When “Rapper’s Delight” came out [in ’79], it set hip-hop back five years.
refs.para: DJ Charlie Chase (Cold Crush Brothers): When “Rapper’s Delight” came out [in ’79], it set hip-hop back five years. Hip-hop started in ’73. In ’77, that shit was preschool for us at that point. We were already rhyming.
refs.chapter: Cap. 3: What in the World Is This?

refs.q: It was a party culture. “Rapper’s Delight” converts it now to a recording culture with the emphasis on the rapper, and it’s completely different.
refs.para: Bill Stephney (Bomb Squad, Def Jam): It was a party culture. “Rapper’s Delight” converts it now to a recording culture with the emphasis on the rapper, and it’s completely different. We lose the ability of a DJ to search the globe far and wide for the perfect beat and to soak the label off of that vinyl, because you want to be the only one who’s now found that perfect beat that’s going to rock the party. What does that even have to do with anything that’s going on today? That’s like coming from the days of the pyramids with how far away and distinct that period was.
refs.chapter: Cap. 3: What in the World Is This?
